asDecan.p: Leo gets cut into three slices of ten degrees, and your Sun is in the last one, somewhere between 20 and 29 degrees. The Golden Dawn gave that slice to Mars. Mars has no particular standing in Leo. It isn't at home there and it isn't weakened either, so it behaves like a guest in the Sun's house and picks up some of the Sun's manners. Both are fire, which helps them get on. Mars brings the readiness to fight, and Leo brings the pride that decides what's worth fighting for. The first slice, the Five of Wands, is Saturn and a lot of scrappy effort. The Six is Jupiter and the victory parade. By the Seven the parade's over and somebody wants your spot, so you're up on the ridge with one stick. It's also the end of the sign, with Virgo coming next, and late Leos tend to carry a bit of Virgo's eye for detail. Strength is your Sun card, and this one is the finer grain inside it.

You notice very quickly when someone's edging onto your ground. A new hire starts copying your manager into emails about a project you set up, and by lunchtime you've drafted the reply in your head. At a family dinner your uncle has a go at your job, or your haircut, or the fact you still rent, and you don't let it slide the way your sister does. You answer him, politely, with facts. In a group chat where everyone's piling onto one friend, you're usually the one who types 'hang on, that's a bit unfair' and then watches the dots appear. None of this feels like aggression from the inside. It feels like basic housekeeping. Mars in the Sun's sign fights out in the open, so people always know where you stand, and to be honest you'd find it hard to hide even if you tried.

Courage is the obvious gift. The less obvious one is that you don't need a crowd behind you. Plenty of people will stand up for something once the room has turned their way. You'll do it at five to one, in a body corporate meeting where everyone wants the cheaper quote and you're the only person who read the engineer's report. Have a look at the man on the card. He's outnumbered, his shoes don't even match, and he's still up there. What that does for other people is easy to miss. Once you've said the unpopular thing, someone quieter usually says 'actually, I agree', and they'd never have gone first. You're also right a fair bit of the time, because by the last degrees of Leo the sign has picked up a little of Virgo's habit of checking the details before it picks a fight.

Choosing the wrong hill is the known risk. The quieter trouble is that you can get so used to the ridge that peace makes you twitchy. A few months with nothing to push against, a job where everyone agrees with you, a relationship that's simply going well, and you'll find something anyway. The neighbour's new fence starts to look like a statement. Then there's conceding small points. You'll give way on the big things if someone properly shows you you're wrong, but the tiny ones, who said they'd book the restaurant, whether the film started at seven or half past, you defend like a border. Apologies tend to come out sideways, as a cup of tea left on someone's desk or the dishes done without being asked, and the person who was waiting for the actual words doesn't always get them.

Hit this decan with a loss or an unfair review and the first thing it does is fight. You ring HR the same afternoon, you write the long email, you tell your partner exactly what you should have said in the meeting and then tell them again in the car. There's a lot of heat in that first day and some of it is useful. A week later the heat usually hasn't gone anywhere. It's moved into your shoulders and your sleep, and you're still holding the ridge against people who've mostly moved on. The ones closest to you get tired of hearing about it, and a few start to feel that disagreeing with you on anything is risky. What helps is physical first. Mars needs somewhere to go, so a hard run or a long swim does more for you than another conversation. After that, ask someone you trust whether this one is still worth holding.

You're the partner who'll take someone's side at a wedding before you know what the argument was about, and most people find that quite romantic for a while. The less obvious bit is that you need to be pushed back on. Someone who agrees with everything bores you within a couple of months, though you'd never admit it, because Mars likes a bit of resistance and without it you go looking for some in the wrong places. You do best with a person who'll argue with you over dinner and have forgotten it by dessert. What trips you up is losing gracefully at home. A partner who says 'you were a bit sharp with my mum' needs to hear 'yeah, I was', and that short sentence costs you far too much. Practise it on small things, like the wrong turn you insisted on or the bin you swore you'd put out.

You work best when there's something specific to hold. A brand you built, a budget line, a client you brought in, a standard nobody else will keep. Give you that and you'll defend it through three restructures. Jobs that suit this slice of Leo often have some advocacy in them, the lawyer, the union delegate, the editor who won't let marketing rewrite the headline, the head chef who sends a plate back. It goes wrong in the job with no clear ground, all consensus and shared ownership and workshops, where you end up defending things that were never yours to begin with. Keep an eye on the moment a colleague's suggestion lands as an attack on your work. Usually it isn't one. When it genuinely is, put your case in writing, calmly, with the numbers, because late Leo is far more persuasive on paper once the heat has had a night to settle.

At twenty this decan fights almost everything. The lecturer who marked you down, the flatmate who used your milk, the manager who didn't listen in your first week. A lot of it is fair, and some of it is just Mars in a young body with nowhere to put it. By the mid-thirties most people with a late Leo Sun have lost a couple of fights that mattered and won a couple that didn't, and that's usually what teaches the sorting. You get choosier. You still stand up, but you've learnt to wait a day first. The fifties often bring a funny shift. Having been the one on the ridge for so long, you become the person others ring when they're outnumbered, and a lot of your fighting gets done on someone else's behalf. I've seen this decan make very good mentors, especially for people starting out in a field that isn't kind to newcomers.

Before you answer a challenge, a snippy email, a comment at dinner, a rival's pitch, give it a score out of ten for how much it actually matters to you. Write the number on a sticky note if it's a message, or just say it in your head. Anything under six gets a short, friendly reply or none at all. Six and above, you fight properly, but you sleep on it first and answer in the morning. Keep a tally for a month and count how many sixes there really were.
